title: Senta’s ballad
where: *The Flying Dutchman*, Act 2, Scene 1, with lines from Acts 1, 2 and 3
about: Senta is the daughter of Daland, a Norwegian sea captain. At home, among girls who sit spinning, she looks at a picture of a pale man in black and sings them the ballad of the Flying Dutchman, which she has often heard from her nurse, Mary. The Dutchman is a captain damned to sail without end; every seven years he may land to seek a wife. Her father has just met him on the coast and promised him his daughter.

view.says: Auden left no account of this opera alone. He called Nietzsche the best guide to Wagner. Nietzsche, he wrote, saw one theme return in one opera after another: someone wants to be saved. Here, as Nietzsche has it, marriage saves even the Wandering Jew and settles him down. Auden’s own Wagner, in *New Year Letter* (1941), stages a hero who roars for his mother or for death, and Woman, who redeems.
view.quote: And Woman, passive as in dreams, / Redeems, redeems, redeems, redeems.
view.source: “The Greatest of the Monsters” (1969), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 253–54; *New Year Letter* (1941), as printed in *The Collected Poetry of W. H. Auden* (New York: Random House, 1945), p. 308
view.checked: read in the scan of Forewords and Afterwords, research/auden/fa.txt, lines 12139–12165 (the passage from Nietzsche begins on p. 253 and its sentence on this opera stands on p. 254), and in the page image of The Collected Poetry (1945) at the Internet Archive (in.ernet.dli.2015.215337, leaf n326, which has 308 printed at its foot; the comma after dreams is plain there, where the machine-read text of the scan has a full stop), both on 2026-10-03; both are also given in the research notes, C section 29

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: six lines of eight syllables and four beats, the first four with a beat on every second syllable; then a close of six beats, where after the cry two syllables come before each beat
lenses.caption: Wagner wrote the words himself. Four lines keep one measure, eight syllables with a beat on every second one, while they tell of the ship and its master on watch. Then three lines start on a beat: the cry Hui, which imitates air rushing past. Outside the ballad only the Dutchman’s crew cry it, in Act 3. The two lines about the wind end on the call Johohe, marked here as the printed tune has it: two short notes, then a long one. After the last Hui every beat has two syllables before it, and the tune gives each pair two quick notes. That line says he flies like an arrow.
lenses.why: The measure is steady while the ballad describes the ship; at the cry Hui the lines begin on the beat, and where he flies like an arrow two syllables, sung as quick notes, come before each beat.

points.say: Said aloud, the first two lines can each begin on a stress: the verb of the question, then *Blut*, blood. The measure puts its beat on the second syllable. In the tune printed in an 1895 libretto the first syllable is a short note before the bar line, the highest of its phrase.

Wagner’s own edition of 1871 prints the close as two lines of three beats each: the cry and the arrow, then the three phrases that begin with *ohne*. This libretto runs them into one long line and carries the last two words over.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: The first four lines rhyme by turns: an with Mann, Mast with Rast. A handbook of English verse calls four-beat lines rhymed this way closely similar to the ballad stanza, and Wagner heads the song Ballade. The two lines about the wind end on the same call. The last word, Ruh, the rest he is without, has no rhyme. What ties it to Rast is its first letter: ohne Rast und Ruh, without halt or rest, is a set phrase that Goethe and Schiller also use. In 1851 Wagner wrote that end rhyme was a deceit and that for his Siegfried he had turned to verse rhymed on first sounds.
lenses.why: The telling lines rhyme by turns, much as a ballad stanza does; the last word, Ruh, the rest he lacks, has no rhyme and is held to Rast by its first letter, the binding Wagner later preferred to rhyme.

grounds.claim: rows 1.0 to 1.3 rhyme a b a b; rows 1.4 and 1.5 end on the same word; Ruh rhymes with no line of the stanza; Rast and Ruh begin with the same letter

lenses.caption: Three phrases that begin with ohne, without, close the stanza. Ziel is a marksman’s mark and a voyage’s end: the line likens him to an arrow and takes the mark away. Rast is a halt on a journey. Ruh is stillness, peace and, in Grimm’s dictionary, the rest found in death. In Act 1 the Dutchman says damnation denies him grave and death; in Act 2 he asks Senta whether her faithfulness will bring the long-desired Ruh. Auden sets the Flying Dutchman beside Ishmael, the exile and the Wandering Jew as names of one figure. Of the Romantic view of the sea he writes that no lasting destination is known.
lenses.why: The close names what he is without: a mark, a halt and rest, a word German also uses of death and the Dutchman of what Senta’s troth may bring; Auden lists him beside the exile and the Wandering Jew.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: Wagner’s first line asks the hearers a question: did you come upon the ship at sea. The English tells it as a fact.
The ship’s master keeps watch without a halt. The English leaves out the watch and describes his eyes and his face; its *pale* comes from the line above in Wagner.
*Hui* imitates rushing air. *Huzza* was first a sailor’s shout of high spirits, encouragement or applause.
Wagner’s word is *er*, he. The ship is *das Schiff*, neuter, so *er* does not point to it; at this place in the second stanza it is the damned man who sails. In the English the ship, *she*, leaps.
With the two words carried below, these phrases name three things he is without: a mark to reach, a halt, rest. The English has two words for endless time.

lenses.caption: Beside Wagner’s stanza stands the English of a New York libretto that names no translator. Its first four lines keep his eight syllables, his rhyme by turns and the ship’s colors. They give up his question to the hearers and the watch without a halt. At the close his er, he, flies like an arrow; in the English the ship, she, leaps forever. Auden’s objection to opera in translation lies elsewhere. In song, he believed, a listener hears syllables, not words: Wagner sung in English is intolerable, and would be even if the translation were the better poem, because the new syllables do not suit the pitch and pace of the notes.
lenses.why: In its first four lines the English keeps Wagner’s count and rhyme and changes what the lines say; Auden held that Wagner in English fails for another reason, the fit of syllable to note, however good the translation.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: Wagner: a woman true to him until death. The English: a woman’s heart that does not fail in its mission.
Wagner turns to the man himself: *du*, you, pale seaman. The English goes on with *he*.

The girls ask where he will meet the woman who would stay his own, true until death (*treueigen*, a compound from the love poetry of Wagner’s century). The English woman is to win his love and share his treasures.
*Treu* is troth, faith kept, kin to English *true*. The English has *love*. The third stanza of the ballad keeps the two apart: false love, false troth.
Senta asks that God’s angel show her to him. In the English she asks the angel to bring him to her.
Wagner: through me you shall reach salvation. The English line describes the man at sea.

lenses.caption: The first five lines are the refrain, the returning part, sung after the first stanza. The last five are sung in its place after the third: two by the girls, three by Senta. The small lines are the libretto’s English. Twice here Wagner names the condition of the Dutchman’s rescue: a woman true bis in den Tod, until death. The English keeps a true woman and both times leaves the death out; its woman is to win his love and share his treasures. In Act 3 the Dutchman says that only a woman true to him until death can free him, and in her last line Senta calls herself true to him until death.
lenses.why: The libretto’s English keeps the true woman and both times leaves out Wagner’s until death, the term of the condition that the Dutchman states in Act 3 and Senta’s last line repeats.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: apostrophe
lenses.plain: a turning away: the speaker turns from the hearers to speak to someone or something else
lenses.caption: The refrain begins by telling of him: the pale man, er, he. Its third line addresses him, du, you, pale seaman; a stage direction that Wagner’s own edition prints after this refrain has Senta turn to his picture toward the end of the stanza, which there takes in the refrain. Then she turns back to her hearers: Betet, pray. In the lines sung at the end the girls too say you to him, and Senta says a word the ballad has used once before, in his oath: Ich, I. She asks to be the woman the song has prayed for. Nietzsche, Auden’s best guide to Wagner, saw one theme return in opera after opera: someone wants to be saved.
lenses.why: The refrain turns from telling of him to addressing him, as Senta turns to his picture, and at the end she answers its prayer with I; the theme Auden reports from Nietzsche is here: someone wants to be saved.

apostrophe is a turning of one’s speech from one audience to another, most often to an abstraction, to an inanimate object or to the absent; the word is from the Greek for a turning away
grounds.source: Gideon O. Burton, Silva Rhetoricae (Brigham Young University), under apostrophe; Online Etymology Dictionary, under apostrophe (n.2)

lenses.label: Verbs
lenses.caption: Only one thing in the refrain is stated as fact: Erlösung, redemption, a setting free, kann, can, still come to him. All that concerns the woman is condition, question or wish: Fänd’, if he found; when will you find her; pray that a woman may keep faith. The girls ask where she is. Senta answers in the wish form too: sei, let me be, as in long live the king. Then she promises: sollst, you shall. Her first line ends on the verb erlösen, to redeem. In Auden’s lines on Wagner that verb is Woman’s, four times over. In the last scene her sei becomes bin, am.
lenses.why: The refrain states that he can be saved and leaves the woman to if, when and may; Senta steps into that wish form with let me be, then promises, and her verb is the one Auden gives Woman: redeem.

grounds.claim: the verbs marked by their form in four kinds: one statement (its two verb words); six verbs in the forms of what is supposed or wished (two past subjunctives, four present subjunctives); three questions; two promises. The order to pray in row 2.3 is not marked here; the Figure tab marks it

lenses.caption: When the curtain rises Wagner’s stage direction has Senta sunk in dreamy contemplation of the picture. After the first stanza she sings the refrain alone; after the second the girls softly join its close; after the third she sinks back and the girls sing on. Then, carried away, she springs up with her own lines. Afterward she has heard nothing of what was said and starts like one waking, and while Erik tells his dream she sinks, the direction says, as into a magnetic sleep. In Auden’s lines on Wagner, Woman redeems while passive, as one is in dreams.
lenses.why: Wagner’s directions have Senta sunk in dreamy contemplation before the ballad and starting like one waking after it; between, the refrain passes to her hearers and she breaks in carried away; Auden’s Woman redeems while passive, as in dreams.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Three places in the opera share one rhyme. Two lines are the Dutchman’s in Act 1, four are Senta’s in Act 2, two are her last words. Each time Tod, death, rhymes with Gebot, command; the libretto has that noun once in each act, always in this rhyme. First the command is damnation’s and forbids him death. He says he has sought death, and in Auden’s lines the Wagner hero roars for it. In Senta’s lines Tod ends the phrase that means until death, the limit of her Treue, troth, and the two words begin alike. After the last Tod the stage direction has her leap into the sea and his ship sink at once.
lenses.why: One rhyme, death with command, ties the Dutchman’s sentence to Senta’s vow and her last cry: the death that the first command forbids him is the term she sets to her troth, and Auden’s Wagner hero roars for death.

lenses.caption: Gebot is a command, and the word for each of the Ten Commandments. It has a different owner each time. In Act 1 it is damnation’s: no grave and no death. In Act 2 it is troth’s, and Senta says she knows it: troth until death. At the end it is his angel’s. In Act 1 the Dutchman speaks of an angel of God who won him the condition of his rescue, and in Act 3 he states that condition: only a woman true until death can free him from the curse. Her last line begins with Hier, here, and gives the condition back: true to you until death.
lenses.why: The same word, command, passes from damnation to troth to the angel, and Senta’s last line repeats in her own person the condition the Dutchman has stated: true until death.

auden.says: In *The Enchafèd Flood* the Flying Dutchman is one of four names Auden gives to a single figure; the others are Ishmael, the exile and the Wandering Jew. That figure is one half of a double-natured hero he finds in a dream told by Wordsworth. The other half is Don Quixote, the dedicated man.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), p. 5
auden.checked: read in the scan, research/auden/ef.txt, lines 296–307, on 2026-10-03; the page follows from the running heads and from the numbers printed at the foot of pp. 10 to 13

auden.says: In the same book he lists what is new in the Romantic attitude to the sea. Every man of feeling and honor wants to leave land and city. Man’s true state is the voyage, and the sea is his real situation. What is decisive happens at sea: the choice that counts forever, temptation, fall and redemption. Life on shore is always trivial. Whether there is a lasting destination nobody knows, and a lasting bond can be neither had nor wished for. He does not apply the list to this opera.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 12–13
auden.checked: read in the scan, research/auden/ef.txt, lines 570–600, on 2026-10-03; the numbers 12 and 13 stand at the foot of the pages

auden.says: In the 1969 essay he calls Wagner’s operas freaks, which have to be listened to differently from most operas. Wagner, he writes, expected his heroes and heroines to be admired, and what he in fact shows is a line of ill-bred neurotics, drawn with the greatest skill. No one else paints what in people is unreasoning, sick, cranky and bent on its own ruin as it really is, with its spell on it. To get the full good of the operas a listener has to find all this in himself and at the same moment hold it at a distance, as what he must overcome.
auden.source: “The Greatest of the Monsters” (1969), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 253 and 255
auden.checked: read in the scan, research/auden/fa.txt, lines 12130–12136 and 12222–12250, on 2026-10-03; the scan drops most punctuation

auden.says: In his own prose note to the lines on Wagner in *New Year Letter*, Auden ranks Wagner first among the Romantic artists. He calls the operas masterpieces when they are taken as studies of tribulation, like a psychoanalyst’s case histories, and absurd when they are taken as dramatic plots, because the characters know beforehand that their mistakes are mistakes; his example is the *Ring*. In giving voice to suffering, he writes, Wagner may be the greatest genius there has been, and his genius stops there.
auden.source: his note to line 1432 of *New Year Letter* (London: Faber, 1941), pp. 143–44; read only in snippets of a scanned copy, with a gap
auden.checked: read only in the research notes, remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, appendix H6, which pieces the note together from search snippets of the Faber edition and leaves a gap; the book was not opened in this session

auden.says: In “Notes on Music and Opera” he writes that a librettist’s verses are meant, like a private letter, for the composer and not for the public, and that, as he believes, people listening to song hear syllables, not words. That is his reason for being, in general, against opera sung in translation. In English, he says, Wagner or Strauss sounds intolerable, and a translation that was the better poem would not help, because the new syllables do not suit the pitch and speed of the notes that carry them.
auden.quote: In song, poetry is expendable, syllables are not.
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 473
auden.checked: read in the scan, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 22250–22290, on 2026-10-03; the running head of p. 473 stands above the passage

auden.says: In the same notes he says that what opera imitates is human willfulness. Music, he writes, is immediate, and nothing merely potential or passive can live beside it; what the great operatic roles share is that each is a state of passion and will. What is sung is so, and for that reason there can be no self-deception in opera. A good libretto plot gives its characters every possible occasion to be carried away, and the theory of music-drama needs a libretto without one sensible moment, which Wagner managed.
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 470–72

caveats: Nothing Auden said about this opera by itself is on record. The view at the head of the page is put together from his essay of 1969 and from lines of 1941 that describe Wagner’s dramas in general.

The German shown is that of an American libretto and differs in places from the text Wagner printed in 1871. There Senta’s first line of her own reads, in English: let me be the one who redeems you through her troth.

The last return of the refrain, at the end of Scene 2, differs by edition: Wagner’s text gives its last three lines whole, a libretto of 1901 that agrees with the score breaks off before the last word, and the libretto shown here gives Senta the girls’ two lines.

The stresses marked are one reader’s hearing. The first word of each of the first two lines, and *wacht* in the fourth, can fairly be given more weight or less. The tune was read in the melody printed in a libretto of 1895, not in a score.
In the arrow line *er*, he, is taken to be the pale man, as at the same place in the second stanza. Grammar rules out the ship, which is neuter. It does not rule out the wind, which is masculine too.
open: Nothing is on record of what Auden said about this opera in the 1941 class. The view is put together from an essay of 1969 and from lines of 1941 that describe Wagner’s dramas in general.

The plates show the German of an American libretto, which differs in places from Wagner’s own text of 1871. In the first of Senta’s three lines on the second plate, Wagner’s text and the 1901 libretto that agrees with the score say: let me be the one who redeems you through her troth. The wording shown, with das Weib and soll, is that of the American librettos (Rullman, and Ditson 1895), and where it came from was not found. The captions lean on sei, Mög’, mich and sollst, which both wordings have; the bold word erlösen and the mark on soll exist only in the wording shown.

Other differences from Wagner’s text of 1871: the close of each stanza is two lines there and one long line here; the third line of the refrain ends in a question mark there and an exclamation mark here; Wagner has einstens for einst; and the last line of the opera reads there, in English, see me here, true to you until death, where the text shown and the libretto of 1901 have here I stand.

The last return of the refrain, at the end of Scene 2, differs by edition: it is complete in Wagner’s text of 1871, breaks off before its last word in the libretto of 1901, and is replaced by the girls’ question in the libretto shown here.

The stage directions in the Scene table are from Wagner’s edition of 1871. The hosted English has no stage directions in Act 2, so a reader cannot check them on the site; the table’s "read" keys point to the nearest speech in the English.
The tune was read only in the melody printed with the words in the Ditson libretto of 1895, not in a score.

The scansion marks one way of saying the lines. A voice can also stress the first word of the first two lines, or wacht in the fourth, more or less than is marked. Johohe is stressed on its last syllable after the way it is sung.
In the arrow line the word er, he, is taken for the pale man, as at the same place in the second stanza. It cannot be the ship, which is neuter; the wind and the mast are masculine nouns too.

No English stands beside the third plate, because its eight lines lie in three acts of the hosted English. There the word for command is law in Act 1 and demands in Act 2, and the last couplet has neither angel nor command.
The compounds Schreck-Gebot and Hochgebot are in neither dictionary; they are glossed from their parts.

The scan of Forewords and Afterwords drops most punctuation, so Auden’s prose there is paraphrased and not quoted. The lines from New Year Letter are quoted from the page image of The Collected Poetry (1945), p. 308, with the punctuation printed there; the London edition of 1941 was not seen, and by the research notes it prints Death and Mother with capitals.
Auden’s prose note of 1941 was read only in the research notes. The Swarthmore chart of 1943 is no longer on the page: its entry was taken out of the list and is kept in notes.md.
The verse handbook cited describes English verse. It is used for the stanza form and for alliteration, not for German stress.

The count of Hui is of the German libretto shown (nine lines of the ballad, three of the chorus of the Dutchman’s crew). The examiner counted again: Wagner’s text of 1871 has it on the same nine lines and three; the libretto of 1901 that agrees with the score, and the hosted English, have it five times in that chorus. In all of them no one but Senta, in the ballad, and the Dutchman’s crew cries it.
